tEn: Stop Planning for 2027: How OpenAI Ships Product in 90-Day Cycles
tZh: 别为 2027 做规划：OpenAI 如何以 90 天为周期打造产品
sEn: OpenAI's Tara Seshan and Nan Yu on shipping imperfect AI products fast, the toggle tradeoff, and why user absorption, not model capability, is the real constraint.
sZh: OpenAI 的 Tara Seshan 与 Nan Yu 谈如何快速交付不完美的 AI 产品、开关式方案的取舍，以及为何真正的瓶颈是用户吸收能力而非模型能力。

consensus.en: Urgency matters: ship imperfect products to get empirical evidence and iterate quickly.
consensus.zh: 紧迫性很重要：发布不完美的产品以获取实证反馈并快速迭代。

consensus.en: Build for where models will be in 2-3 months, not overly anchored in present or future.
consensus.zh: 为模型2-3个月后的能力而构建，不要过度锚定当下或未来。

consensus.en: User empathy and systems thinking remain core, plus relentlessness to iterate.
consensus.zh: 用户同理心和系统思维仍是核心，加上不懈迭代的韧性。

consensus.en: Onboarding and user understanding of privacy and norms are newly table stakes.
consensus.zh: 用户引导以及用户对隐私和规范的理解成为新的基本要求。

consensus.en: Direct user relationships (DMable PM) are increasingly important for product leaders.
consensus.zh: 直接的用户关系（可私信的产品经理）对产品领导者越来越重要。

consensus.en: Voice will be a major product form factor by 2027 due to natural interaction.
consensus.zh: 到2027年，语音将因自然交互而成为主要产品形态。

contrarian.en: Enterprises can't absorb change is broken; not shipping frontier risks being leapfrogged.
contrarian.zh: 企业无法吸收变化的说法已过时；不发布前沿产品就有被颠覆的风险。

contrarian.en: Single identity agents may not scale; grouping into bundles like chief of staff is key.
contrarian.zh: 单一身份智能体可能无法扩展；像幕僚长一样分组打包是关键。

contrarian.en: Computer use always finishes the job, beating 99% solutions that fail last mile.
contrarian.zh: 计算机使用总能完成任务，胜过99%但最后一公里失败的方案。

contrarian.en: Annual planning beyond 90 days is futile for fast-moving AI businesses.
contrarian.zh: 对于快速变化的AI业务，超过90天的年度规划是徒劳的。

contrarian.en: Products should use themselves to solve empty input box, like self-driving on-ramp.
contrarian.zh: 产品应能自我使用以解决空输入框问题，如同自动驾驶的平滑接入。

turns.en: All right, we're here. And I warned them backstage what we were going to start this talk about because I know there's a lot of questions about OpenAI. There's a lot of questions about the future of product development. But what I want to talk about is—
turns.zh: 好了，我们开始了。我在后台就警告过他们我们要从什么话题开始，因为我知道有很多关于 OpenAI 的问题。有很多关于产品开发未来的问题。但我想谈的是——

turns.en: What do you want to talk about, Claire?
turns.zh: 你想谈什么，Claire？

turns.en: The toggle. I want to talk about the fact that every AI product has two faces. It has left toggle and right toggle. And there's been a lot of conversation today about iterative product development and shipping things that are imperfect and getting things into the wild. And so Tara, I just want you to talk to me about shipping imperfect things instead of a toggle and how do you make these decisions about putting things in the wild that you know may not be the perfect thing right now but are the right thing ultimately to build the right product.
turns.zh: 那个开关。我想谈谈每个 AI 产品都有两张脸。它有左开关和右开关。今天有很多关于迭代产品开发、发布不完美的东西、把东西推向市场的讨论。所以 Tara，我想请你跟我聊聊发布不完美的东西而不是一个开关，以及你如何做出这些决定，把你知道现在可能不是完美的东西、但最终是正确的东西推向市场，以构建正确的产品。

turns.en: For sure. I will say this to start: I'm the daughter of Asian parents. I'm not used to doing imperfect things. You have to output something perfect every time. I also worked at Stripe for like seven some odd years and everything at Stripe is deeply polished and deeply considered—did you think through it 100 times and did you name this enum the exact correct thing? And I think what has been a big change about shipping things in this era is actually urgency really matters in terms of getting the functionality out there. And also there's a lot of theorizing that one can do before you ship something, but nothing compares to the actual empirical evidence of seeing users try it, use it, and then iterating from there. So I've really had to shift my mindset from how do you get it perfect a priori versus how do you ship something and iterate on it as quickly and effectively as possible. So with the toggle, is it the perfect solution? No, it is an imperfect solution. It is certainly not the ideal thing to ship. But what was really important was getting this agentic harness—or the ability to use an agent to get things done—in the hands of the over a billion users that use ChatGPT. And so we needed to ship something that allowed us to do that without disrupting developers' workflows.
turns.zh: 当然。我先说这一点：我是亚洲父母的孩子。我不习惯做不完美的事情。你每次都必须输出完美的东西。我也在 Stripe 工作了大约七年，Stripe 的一切都经过深度打磨和深思熟虑——你有没有想过 100 遍，你有没有把这个枚举命名得完全正确？我认为在这个时代发布东西的一个重大变化是，紧迫性真的很重要，要把功能推向市场。而且，在发布之前你可以做很多理论化的工作，但没有什么能比看到用户尝试、使用，然后从中迭代的实际经验证据更重要。所以我真的不得不转变心态，从如何先验地做到完美，转变为如何发布东西并尽可能快速有效地迭代。所以关于那个开关，它是完美的解决方案吗？不，它是不完美的解决方案。它当然不是理想的发布产品。但真正重要的是把这个智能体框架——或者说使用智能体完成任务的能力——交到超过十亿使用 ChatGPT 的用户手中。所以我们需要发布一些东西，让我们能够做到这一点，同时不破坏开发者的工作流程。

turns.en: As such an imperfect solution. And you know what, I do believe that in a year maybe we won't be having the same conversation about the struggle. And we've had this chat before where we've talked about right now you have to build and throw away a lot of stuff, whether it's code or product. And I'm curious how you think about deciding what to deprecate and what to keep around and keep alive.
turns.zh: 作为如此不完美的解决方案。你知道吗，我确实相信一年后我们可能不会再进行同样的关于挣扎的对话。我们之前也聊过，现在你必须构建并丢弃很多东西，无论是代码还是产品。我很好奇你如何决定废弃什么、保留什么并保持活力。

turns.en: You know, the toggle is a good example of this where I think there's an obvious sort of next step which is like no toggle, right? Like there's a story that evolves from step A to step B. And if you can take users on the journey with you, then they're a lot more accepting of the change and the turn and the product evolution. Especially if they appreciate that they can have an understanding and some transparency over what's actually going on behind the scenes. So I think as long as you have a coherent story that users can follow along with and, with the amount of attention that they're paying, there's actually a lot that you can do and not really burn any kind of bridges with them.
turns.zh: 你知道，那个开关就是一个很好的例子，我认为有一个明显的下一步，就是没有开关，对吧？就像有一个从步骤 A 到步骤 B 的故事。如果你能带着用户一起踏上旅程，那么他们就会更容易接受变化、转折和产品演进。特别是如果他们欣赏他们能够理解并有一定透明度地了解幕后实际发生的事情。所以我认为，只要你有一个连贯的故事，用户能够跟随，并且考虑到他们投入的注意力，你实际上可以做很多事情，而不会真正烧毁任何桥梁。

turns.en: Yeah. And I'm curious, you know, that the toggle is maybe imperfect and we may build a lot of stuff that we have to throw away, but you do exercise good judgment and you do exercise caution and reason inside the products that you've worked on or are about to work on. What constraints do you hold really strongly when building product that's moving so fast? What keeps that quality bar high for you?
turns.zh: 是的。我很好奇，你知道，那个开关可能不完美，我们可能构建很多必须丢弃的东西，但你在你曾经或即将从事的产品中确实运用了良好的判断力，也确实运用了谨慎和理性。在如此快速发展的产品构建中，你坚持哪些约束？是什么让你保持高质量标准？

turns.en: I think there's a few different elements of it. One is certainly: are we doing something additive for users? Are we unlocking additional value? Is there something genuinely useful in this product? I think the second is that we have this internal bar of taking a product, shipping it internally, trying it out, having everyone use it, and if there isn't enough uptake internally—and that's not a specific number or exact bar—but there is: is it retaining well? Do people find something delightful about it or something surprisingly great about it? Is it unlocking a new use case of the models? Is it doing something novel? I think that sense for this is adding to their experience. This is something that is unlocking a new set of functionality. And then probably most importantly in this era is: is this aiming for 2 to 3 months of where the models will be, rather than being overly anchored in the present or being overly futuristic and unusable? Is this at that perfect zone of being—I don't know—sufficiently AGI-pilled, that I think is the bar here. So: is it valuable? Do users care about it? Is it surprisingly great for users? And is it in line with model capabilities? And is it getting out of the way of the model doing a great job?
turns.zh: 我认为有几个不同的要素。一个当然是：我们是否在为使用者做加法？我们是否在释放额外价值？这个产品里是否有真正有用的东西？第二个是我们有一个内部标准：拿一个产品，内部发布，试用，让所有人使用，如果内部采用率不够——这不是一个具体的数字或确切的标准——但有一个标准：留存好吗？人们是否发现它令人愉悦或出乎意料地棒？它是否解锁了模型的新用例？它是否在做一些新颖的事情？我认为那种感觉是：这是在增加他们的体验。这是在解锁一组新功能。然后在这个时代可能最重要的是：这是否瞄准了模型 2 到 3 个月后的状态，而不是过度锚定于现在或过度未来主义而无法使用？这是否处于那个完美的区域——我不知道——足够 AGI 化，我认为这就是这里的标准。所以：它有价值吗？用户关心吗？对用户来说是否出乎意料地棒？它是否与模型能力一致？它是否让模型不受阻碍地发挥出色？

turns.en: Nan, what about you? What constraints do you think help you build great product?
turns.zh: Nan，你呢？你认为哪些约束有助于你构建出色的产品？

turns.en: The biggest constraint is honestly people's understanding and ability to absorb what you're giving them, right? We talk a lot about capability overhang, but models can do so much and people aren't necessarily taking advantage of all those abilities. I think that's where the gap is, right? So it doesn't matter what you put into it, if the ability for people to absorb those changes and absorb that capability isn't there, then that's the real bounding process that you're dealing with.
turns.zh: 最大的约束老实说是人们的理解力和吸收你所提供内容的能力，对吧？我们经常谈论能力过剩，但模型能做这么多，人们不一定在利用所有这些能力。我认为这就是差距所在，对吧？所以无论你投入什么，如果人们吸收这些变化和吸收那种能力的能力不存在，那么这就是你面临的真正约束过程。

turns.en: You know, and we're talking right now, you two are working on codecs and work and there's a lot of business users including myself that have built businesses around relying on this tool and I think you know I spent a minute and a half in enterprise and a lot of people say that B2B customers cannot absorb change. I mean like customer success people tell me they can't absorb change. Sales people tell me sales people can't absorb change. Like we cannot absorb the rate of change. Do you feel like that still stands true in the AI era or do you feel like that statement is broken right now?
turns.zh: 你知道，我们现在在聊，你们两位正在做 Codecs 和相关工作，有很多商业用户包括我自己都围绕依赖这个工具建立了业务，我想你知道我在企业领域待了一段时间，很多人说 B2B 客户无法吸收变化。我的意思是，客户成功人员告诉我他们无法吸收变化。销售人员告诉我销售人员无法吸收变化。就像我们无法吸收变化的速度。你觉得这在 AI 时代仍然成立，还是你觉得这个说法现在已经被打破了？

turns.en: Some of it is certainly true in that I think the current pace probably to most enterprises feels beyond breakneck—like something beyond breakneck, a la palooza of features and advancements. It certainly feels maybe to some overwhelming. But at the same time, if you're not shipping the latest and the frontier to these enterprises, you'll end up getting leapfrogged. So a great example of this is that most of our enterprises were using chat.
turns.zh: 其中一些确实是真的，我认为当前的速度对大多数企业来说可能感觉快得离谱——就像快得离谱，功能和进步的盛宴。对某些人来说确实感觉可能令人不堪重负。但与此同时，如果你不向这些企业发布最新和前沿的东西，你最终会被超越。一个很好的例子是，我们大多数企业都在使用聊天。

transcript.secZh: 不完美发布与切换开关

turns.en: So they were merely asking questions and getting answers, and whilst that was happening, the agent revolution was going on. We needed to get agents to these enterprises as fast as possible, otherwise they might consider alternative products. While they have their own pace of absorbing changes day to day, we needed to ship this giant revolutionary change that broke all of their processes and broke all of their conceptions about how enterprises should receive new updates, so that they could actually unlock more value. It's one of those things — it's a truism of building product: do what your users need, not what your users say they need. And I think that applies here almost more than it ever has before.
turns.zh: 所以他们只是在提问、得到回答，而与此同时，智能体革命正在发生。我们需要尽快把智能体交付给这些企业，否则他们可能会考虑其他产品。他们有自己的节奏去消化变化，而我们需要交付这个巨大的革命性变化——它打破了他们所有的流程，也打破了他们对企业应如何接收新更新的所有认知，这样他们才能真正释放更多价值。这就是做产品的一条老生常谈：做用户真正需要的，而不是用户嘴上说需要的。我觉得这一点在这里比以往任何时候都更适用。

turns.en: I want to talk about agents since you brought them up, because I do think we're in the age of agents, and I have certainly been in the age of agents for a little bit. And I want to have a debate with you —
turns.zh: 既然你提到了智能体，我想聊聊这个话题，因为我确实觉得我们正处在智能体时代，我自己也已经在智能体时代里待了一阵子了。我想跟你辩论一下——

turns.en: Oh gosh.
turns.zh: 哦天哪。

turns.en: — or I want your opinion. Maybe we won't have a debate, maybe we'll agree. Single-identity agents versus multi-identity agents: my beloved Codex docked on my computer that I talk to all day versus my 40 Grok bots that are load-bearing across different parts of my business. I do think as product builders, people who are building agents, we're seeing this divergence: do we centralize on a central, generic agent identity that can do anything and let the models get out of the way of the models, or do we artisanal-craft soul MDs and have little micro agents for the job? But I'm just curious, coming in with fresh eyes, where do you land, if anywhere, on that spectrum from a design-principles perspective?
turns.zh: ——或者我想听听你的看法。也许我们不用辩论，也许我们会达成一致。单一身份智能体 vs. 多身份智能体：一边是我电脑上那个我整天跟它说话的、我心爱的 Codex，另一边是我那 40 个 Grok 机器人，它们在我业务的不同环节里承担着关键作用。我确实觉得，作为产品构建者、作为做智能体的人，我们正看到这种分化：是把一切集中到一个能做任何事的通用智能体身份上、让模型自己去发挥，还是手工打磨 soul MD、为具体任务做小小的微智能体？但我很好奇，带着新鲜视角来看，从设计原则的角度，你在这个光谱上落在哪里——如果有的话？

turns.en: I think when designing this, the most successful efforts have really tried to map onto human nature, right? We have millions of years of evolution that help us understand how to hold different things in our heads. And 40 agents is quite a lot, right? If you asked anybody, would you manage 40 direct employees — some, you know, Jensen Huang might do it — but a lot of people would kind of look at that and be like, I don't know if I could actually keep up with that many threads ongoing. So I think there's something in there where we need to group these things into bundles of activity. If you ask people, hey, how do you manage your agents? Usually what you'll hear is, well, first I have this chief-of-staff agent that manages all the other ones for me. It's like, okay, you've just cheated, right? You're not managing seven, you're managing one that's kind of running your team. So I think that dynamic immediately comes to the front as soon as you let people do this kind of stuff.
turns.zh: 我觉得在设计这个的时候，最成功的尝试其实都试图贴合人性，对吧？我们有数百万年的进化，帮助我们理解如何在脑子里同时装下不同的东西。而 40 个智能体是相当多的，对吧？你问任何人，你愿意管理 40 个直接下属吗——有些人，比如黄仁勋也许可以——但很多人看到这个都会说，我不确定我能不能真的跟上这么多条并行的线。所以我觉得这里面有个东西：我们需要把这些东西归组成一束束的活动。如果你问人们，嘿，你是怎么管理你的智能体的？通常你会听到的是，嗯，首先我有一个幕僚长智能体，它替我管理其他所有智能体。好吧，你这就是作弊了，对吧？你不是在管理七个，你是在管理一个在替你带团队的东西。所以我觉得，一旦你让人们这么干，这种动态立刻就会浮现出来。

turns.en: What about you? What do you think?
turns.zh: 那你呢？你怎么看？

turns.en: My mind with this — certainly there's a philosophical element to it: do you have this one unified entity, do you have these smaller entities? But actually there are a lot of really tactical questions that go into it, like how do you think about data access and permissions? If you have one entity, is it switching between using a service account or your account? How do you manifest that to the user in an easy way to understand? If you have a single agent, does it have segmented memory — like, every time it joins a private Slack channel, is it almost a different agent? Is it severed in the Slack channel, in the Severance sense? So actually, to me, answering this question goes back to really specifically the use case, and probably thinking through all of those edge cases: how should the memory behave, how should it talk to each person, should it be using their credentials or should it be using a universal set of credentials? There are philosophical things one could opine on in this topic, but to me there are just so many practical product considerations — the use case matters so much in deciding this.
turns.zh: 我的想法是——这里面当然有哲学层面的东西：你是要一个统一的实体，还是要这些更小的实体？但实际上，这里面有很多非常具体的问题，比如你怎么考虑数据访问和权限？如果你有一个实体，它是在服务账号和你自己的账号之间切换吗？你怎么把它以用户容易理解的方式呈现出来？如果你有一个单一智能体，它有分段记忆吗——比如每次它加入一个私密 Slack 频道，它是不是几乎变成了另一个智能体？它在 Slack 频道里是被“分离”了吗，就像《人生切割术》那样？所以对我来说，回答这个问题其实要回到非常具体的用例，并且大概要把所有这些边界情况都想清楚：记忆应该如何表现，它应该如何与每个人对话，它应该用他们的凭证，还是用一套通用凭证？这个话题上当然可以有哲学层面的观点，但对我来说，这里有太多实际的产品考量——用例在决定这件事上太重要了。

turns.en: What I love about these two answers is, I think for product folks — everybody in the audience, plus designers — there are these two sides of the craft that we do. There's this very human side, where you're trying to — there's Inception and Severance, I guess — there's the Inception of how do I get in the mind of a user, what are their mental models, how do they interface with the world, what is the most natural way for our products to touch their problems and solve them. And then there is systems and architect thinking, which is: in order to manifest this into the world in a realistic way, I need to think through all these systems, all these platform components, all these edge cases, to make sure that comprehensively we can even deliver this to the user in a sensible way. Do you think those are the two skill sets you need to design and build great agents in this moment? Are there other hard skills you feel like you're relying on now more than ever as you design or think about agentic experiences?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这两个回答的地方在于，我觉得对产品人——在座所有人，加上设计师——我们这门手艺有这两面。一面是非常人性的一面，你要试着——这里有《盗梦空间》，还有《人生切割术》——有《盗梦空间》那一面：我怎么进入用户的头脑，他们的心智模型是什么，他们如何与世界交互，我们的产品用什么最自然的方式触及并解决他们的问题。然后还有系统与架构思维，也就是：为了把这个东西以现实的方式呈现到世界上，我需要把所有这些系统、所有平台组件、所有边界情况都想清楚，确保我们能以合理的方式把它完整地交付给用户。你觉得这就是当下设计和构建优秀智能体所需要的两种技能吗？还是说，在你设计或思考智能体式体验时，你觉得还有其他硬技能是你现在比以往更依赖的？

turns.en: You're describing systems thinking plus user empathy. These are very classic product-management types of ideas, right, that we applied to a different universe of technology in the before times. But now we have to start from scratch and from those principles rethink how these products want to be shaped. So I think those are very important, but ultimately they're just the old principles in disguise. I would maybe add a thing to that, which is — again, I mentioned I used to work at Stripe, which is a very academic company, and my parents are very academic, and I love thinking about those things in the abstract — but I'd say the third thing you really need, in addition to user empathy and systems thinking, is a relentlessness to try it out and keep iterating, and you're going to take a lot of pain while you do that. There's just an element of relentlessly trying and trying and trying and trying to see what works.

turns.zh: 你知道，我认为重点会变化，对吧？就像有很多原因，但你知道，我们谈到了吸收率和能力过剩。所以我认为现在可能比以前更重要的事情是引导流程。我想我们谈过，你知道，人们谈过引导流程是重要的事情，但它也有点具体，很多工程师不喜欢做这个之类的，但我认为要真正获得很多成功，思考初始体验是什么？你如何让人们真正理解你的产品是什么，这可能是现在比以前重要得多的事情。

turns.en: Tara, what do you think?

tldr.en: Ship imperfect products in 90-day cycles to get empirical evidence and iterate fast.
